vignette: Samira, a fifty-nine-year-old American police officer of Middle Eastern descent, built her career on calculated calm until a masked assailant ambushed her in the patrol station lot. The sudden violence shattered her composure, and as he forced her into the passenger seat, her own heart began racing and pounding in her chest while his weapon filled her vision. That night fused her physiological alarm directly to the event, meaning that whenever her heart races or pounds now, the memory of the assault instantly resurfaces with exceptional clarity. The memories are never fragmented; they remain vivid and detailed, and when they return, she experiences the same crushing terror she felt at the time. Because these intrusive recollections arrive unbidden during routine patrol shifts or whenever she witnesses violence, Samira has come to believe her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger even when she is safe. This physiological betrayal convinces her that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that the department has done nothing about it, which directly fuels her conviction that she can't rely on other people. Convinced she was vulnerable and alone, Samira systematically began to cut off all contact with friends and family, retreating into an empty home where she could control her environment. The vivid, terror-inducing recurrences made social contact feel unbearable, pushing her further into withdrawal. Simultaneously, her appraisal that she can't rely on other people directly caused her to sever relationships, while her belief that her body was an enemy made her constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, treating her mind like a threat that required surveillance. By isolating completely, she deprived herself of corrective experiences, which solidified her negative appraisals of injustice and bodily betrayal. The more she monitored her thoughts, the more convinced she became that her physiology was inherently dangerous, which in turn made her hyper-aware of her heart racing. Her hypervigilance also sharpened her sensitivity to danger cues, which kept her heart racing and pulled her into the cycle. These maladaptive strategies only fed back into her trauma schema: without the buffer of connection, the vivid memories and terror on recall continued to intensify, making the past feel as immediate as the present. This unprocessed recall then cemented her belief that life was fundamentally unjust and that her own body was unreliable, which pushed her to isolate further and police her thoughts more aggressively. The feedback loop tightened relentlessly over the months. Her refusal to drive with others grew into a rigid rule, yet the mere sight of a crowded highway triggered the same physiological alarm, which immediately dragged the auditory memories back with full force. Her framing of the event as a profound injustice kept her constantly on guard for violence, which kept her body primed for threat. That aggressive self-monitoring, in turn, prevented emotional processing, keeping the memories vivid and terror-laden, which kept her attuned to danger, which kept her heart racing. At fifty-nine, the exhaustion of fighting this internal war finally broke her; she sought help after a traffic stop turned into a panic attack, terrified that her mind would never stop screaming warnings. What she hoped for was not to forget the assault, but to finally break the chain where her memories, her appraisals, her avoidance, and her body's alarms continued to feed one another.
